result.markdown: --- title: "Session 3 — Regression with Survey Data" subtitle: "svyglm · quasibinomial · odds ratios · glm vs svyglm · Wald tests · predictions · Lab 3" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Sessions 1 and 2: design, weights, descriptive estimates - Today: **regression** that respects the design - By the end you can: - fit **logistic and linear** models with `svyglm()` - explain why `glm()` gives **similar estimates but wrong SEs** - **test** a multi-level variable with the design - give **predicted probabilities** ::: # Topic 1 — svyglm {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A logistic model for hypertension ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_svy <- svyglm(hypertension ~ age + sex + residence + bmi + wealth, design = des, family = quasibinomial()) round(summary(m_svy)$coefficients, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) -6.474 0.567 -11.410 0.000 age 0.056 0.005 11.940 0.000 sexMale 0.104 0.129 0.807 0.425 residenceUrban 0.726 0.194 3.741 0.001 bmi 0.098 0.018 5.299 0.000 wealth -0.011 0.063 -0.169 0.867 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Same formula as `glm()`; the **design** replaces `data` - `quasibinomial`: weighted data give **non-integer** "successes", so the plain binomial warns; the **SEs come from the design** anyway - Age, BMI and **urban residence** are associated with hypertension; sex and wealth are not, once adjusted ::: ## Odds ratios ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m_svy), confint(m_svy)))[-1, ], 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OR 2.5 % 97.5 % age 1.06 1.05 1.07 sexMale 1.11 0.85 1.44 residenceUrban 2.07 1.39 3.07 bmi 1.10 1.06 1.14 wealth 0.99 0.87 1.12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Per year of age **OR 1.06**; per BMI unit **OR 1.10**; **urban vs rural OR 2.1** (95% CI 1.4 to 3.1), adjusted for the other variables. As always, an **odds** ratio is **not** a risk ratio: hypertension is common here (20%), so it exaggerates the risk ratio. ::: # Topic 2 — Why not just glm()? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Three analyses of the same model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_glm <- glm(hypertension ~ age + sex + residence + bmi + wealth, data = resp, family = binomial) m_w <- glm(hypertension ~ age + sex + residence + bmi + wealth, data = resp, family = quasibinomial, weights = weight / mean(weight)) rbind(`glm (ignores design)` = summary(m_glm)$coefficients["residenceUrban", 1:2], `glm with weights only` = summary(m_w)$coefficients["residenceUrban", 1:2], svyglm = summary(m_svy)$coefficients["residenceUrban", 1:2]) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error glm (ignores design) 0.675 0.134 glm with weights only 0.726 0.143 svyglm 0.726 0.194 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - The **estimates** are close (0.67 to 0.73) - The **SE** of the urban coefficient: **0.13** (ignoring the design), **0.14** (weights only), **0.19** (full design) - Weights alone **fix the bias but not the variance**; **clusters** are what make SEs larger - Rule: **use `svyglm`** for design-based inference; compare with `glm` as a sensitivity check ::: ## Should regression be weighted? ::: {.warn} Some statisticians prefer an **unweighted model** when the model is well specified and includes the variables used for the sampling (e.g. residence): it is more efficient. For **population-level reporting** (prevalence, ORs for a national report), the **design-based** `svyglm` is the safe default. If the two give **very different** coefficients, the model is probably **missing something**. ::: # Topic 3 — Other outcomes and tests {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A continuous outcome ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_lin <- svyglm(sbp ~ age + sex + residence + bmi + wealth, design = des) round(summary(m_lin)$coefficients, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 86.35 2.53 34.19 0.00 age 0.45 0.03 14.23 0.00 sexMale 1.48 0.61 2.43 0.02 residenceUrban 5.81 1.10 5.27 0.00 bmi 0.80 0.13 6.22 0.00 wealth 0.00 0.36 0.00 1.00 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} SBP rises **0.45 mmHg per year** of age, **0.8 mmHg per BMI unit**, and is **5.8 mmHg higher** in urban adults. Default family: gaussian, with design-based SEs. ::: ## Testing a multi-level variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_edu <- svyglm(hypertension ~ age + sex + residence + bmi + wealth + education, design = des, family = quasibinomial()) regTermTest(m_edu, ~education) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Wald test for education in svyglm(formula = hypertension ~ age + sex + residence + bmi + wealth + education, design = des, family = quasibinomial()) F = 2.632794 on 2 and 33 df: p= 0.086924 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - A **Wald test** of all education coefficients together, using the design - p ≈ 0.09: **no clear evidence** of an education effect after adjustment - Likelihood-ratio tests and AIC are **not available** in the usual way for survey models (no true likelihood); use Wald tests ::: ## Predicted probabilities ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nd <- data.frame(age = 50, sex = factor("Male", levels = levels(resp$sex)), residence = factor(c("Rural", "Urban"), levels = levels(resp$residence)), bmi = 26, wealth = 3) round(predict(m_svy, newdata = nd, type = "response"), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 0.26 0.42 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} A 50-year-old man with BMI 26: probability of hypertension about **26% in a rural** and **42% in an urban** area. **Predicted probabilities** are easier for readers than odds ratios: report **both**. ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 3 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `survey-workshop/labs/lab3_regression.R` - `svyglm` logistic model and odds ratios - glm, weights-only glm and svyglm side by side - linear model, `regTermTest`, predictions ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v3q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="g3jx5n.83q40k" data-show="V2VpZ2h0cyBnaXZlIG5vbi1pbnRlZ2VyIGNvdW50cywgYW5kIHRoZSBkZXNpZ24gc3VwcGxp ZXMgdGhlIFNFcw==" data-explain="QSBiaW5vbWlhbCBtb2RlbCB3YXJucyBhYm91dCBub24taW50ZWdlciBzdWNjZXNzZXMgY3Jl YXRlZCBieSB3ZWlnaHRzLiBUaGUgcXVhc2kgZmFtaWx5IGF2b2lkcyB0aGF0LCBhbmQgc3Z5 Z2xtIHRha2VzIHRoZSB2YXJpYW5jZSBmcm9tIHRoZSBkZXNpZ24u"} Why is family = quasibinomial() used for a binary outcome in svyglm? - Weights give non-integer counts, and the design supplies the SEs - It forces the odds ratio of each predictor in the model to lie between zero and one - It is the family that svyglm requires for an outcome coded 0 or 1 - It estimates a dispersion parameter that replaces the design effect ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v3q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="g3kaee.83qihz" data-show="Q2x1c3RlcmluZyBtYWtlcyByZXNwb25kZW50cyBhbGlrZSwgc28gdGhlIGdsbSBTRSBpcyB0 b28gc21hbGw=" data-explain="V2VpZ2h0cyBtYWlubHkgY2hhbmdlIHRoZSBlc3RpbWF0ZS4gVGhlIGNvcnJlbGF0aW9uIG9m IHJlc3BvbmRlbnRzIHdpdGhpbiBQU1VzIG1haW5seSBjaGFuZ2VzIHRoZSB2YXJpYW5jZSwg d2hpY2ggZ2xtIGlnbm9yZXMu"} The glm and svyglm coefficients for urban residence are close, but their SEs differ. Why? - svyglm has a bigger sample, and this raises the standard errors - glm cannot use weights, so its coefficients are biased here - Clustering makes respondents alike, so the glm SE is too small - The glm SE is right, and svyglm makes it conservative to be safe ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v3q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="g3knn2.83qwzb" data-show="SXQgaXMgc3RpbGwgdG9vIHNtYWxsLCBiZWNhdXNlIHRoZSBQU1VzIGFyZSBub3QgdGFrZW4g aW50byBhY2NvdW50" data-explain="V2VpZ2h0cyBhbG9uZSBjb3JyZWN0IHRoZSBwb2ludCBlc3RpbWF0ZS4gQ2x1c3RlcmluZyBh bmQgc3RyYXRpZmljYXRpb24gZW50ZXIgdGhlIHZhcmlhbmNlLCBzbyB0aGUgU0UgbmVlZHMg dGhlIGRlc2lnbi4="} A glm that uses weights = weight but has no clusters gives a coefficient similar to svyglm. What about its SE? - It is correct, because the weights already cover the clustering - It is still too small, because the PSUs are not taken into account - It is too large, because weights inflate the variance of respondents - It cannot be computed, since weights and SEs cannot be combined ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v3q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="g3l0vs.83rbgp" data-show="V2hldGhlciBhbGwgdGhlIGVkdWNhdGlvbiBjb2VmZmljaWVudHMgYXJlIHplcm8sIGFsbG93 aW5nIGZvciB0aGUgZGVzaWdu" data-explain="SXQgaXMgYSBXYWxkIHRlc3Qgb2YgdGhlIHdob2xlIHRlcm0sIHdoaWNoIGhhcyB0d28gY29l ZmZpY2llbnRzIGZvciB0aHJlZSBlZHVjYXRpb24gbGV2ZWxzLCB3aXRoIGEgZGVzaWduLWJh c2VkIHZhcmlhbmNlLg=="} What does regTermTest(model, ~education) test? - Whether education has a different mean in each stratum of the design - Whether the odds ratio of the first education level equals one in the model - Whether all the education coefficients are zero, allowing for the design - Whether education is correlated with the weights of the respondents in the survey ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="v3q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="g3le4i.83rpy3" data-show="VXJiYW4gYWR1bHRzIGhhdmUgYWJvdXQgdHdpY2UgdGhlIG9kZHMgb2YgaHlwZXJ0ZW5zaW9u LCBhZnRlciBhZGp1c3RtZW50" data-explain="VGhlIE9SIGNvbXBhcmVzIG9kZHMuIFdpdGggYSBjb21tb24gb3V0Y29tZSAoMjAlKSB0aGUg cmlzayByYXRpbyBpcyBtdWNoIHNtYWxsZXIgdGhhbiB0aGUgb2RkcyByYXRpbywgc28gJ3R3 aWNlIGFzIGxpa2VseScgb3ZlcnN0YXRlcyB0aGUgZWZmZWN0Lg=="} In the model, the odds ratio for urban residence is 2.1. Which reading is best? - Urban adults are twice as likely to have hypertension as rural adults - Urban adults have an SBP that is twice as high as that of rural adults - Twice as many urban adults as rural adults have hypertension in the population - Urban adults have about twice the odds of hypertension, after adjustment ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **`svyglm(formula, design = des, family = quasibinomial())`** - `glm` gives similar **estimates**, but **SEs too small** - Weights alone fix the bias; **clusters** fix the variance - **`regTermTest`** for multi-level terms; no LR test or AIC - Report **ORs and predicted probabilities** ::: **Next:** Session 4: nonresponse, raking and replicate weights

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
